references.text: Jesus uses the same parable of the mustard seed in Matthew, with the same introductory question form: "What shall we compare the kingdom of God to?" ([ref:Matt 13:31-32|Matthew 13:31-32]).
Mark has a parallel account where Jesus also asks what the kingdom of God can be compared to, using the mustard seed as an image ([ref:Mark 4:30-32|Mark 4:30-32]).
The parable of the mustard seed itself follows immediately after this introductory question and gives the answer to what the kingdom of God is like ([ref:Luk 13:19|Luke 13:19]).

After the mustard seed parable, a new parable about yeast follows, introduced by a similar question: "What shall I compare the kingdom of God to?" – showing that Jesus uses double parables to explain the growth of the kingdom ([ref:Luk 13:20-21|Luke 13:20-21]).
The question form "Who will you compare him with?" in Isaiah forms a background for the rhetorical questioning style Jesus uses about the kingdom of God ([ref:Jes 40:18|Isaiah 40:18]).
Isaiah asks similar rhetorical questions about comparison: "Who will you compare me to?" – a question form that Jesus here applies to the kingdom of God ([ref:Jes 46:5|Isaiah 46:5]).

Ezekiel uses the image of a tree growing from a small twig into a mighty tree where birds dwell – an image that underlies Jesus' parable about the growth of the kingdom of God from something small to something large ([ref:Esek 17:22-23|Ezekiel 17:22-23]).

Daniel's image of the great tree that all the earth could see, and where the birds of heaven lived in its branches, is a background for Jesus' use of the tree metaphor for the kingdom of God ([ref:Dan 4:10-12|Daniel 4:10-12]).
